questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Wound Healing — Keloid vs Hypertrophic Scar
questions.question_text: A 24-year-old dark-skinned woman develops a raised, itchy scar on her ear lobe 3 months after ear piercing. The scar extends well beyond the original wound margins and does not regress. Which of the following BEST distinguishes this lesion from a hypertrophic scar?

options.A: Hypertrophic scar extends beyond wound margins and regresses spontaneously; keloid stays within margins
options.B: Keloid extends beyond wound margins, does not regress spontaneously, contains abundant type III collagen, and has a higher recurrence after excision alone; hypertrophic scar stays within wound margins and may regress over time
options.C: Keloid is due to excess type I collagen deposition while hypertrophic scar involves type III collagen
options.D: Keloid is seen only on the face while hypertrophic scar can occur anywhere

questions.explanation: Keloid vs hypertrophic scar: Keloid — extends BEYOND original wound margins, does NOT regress spontaneously, more common in dark-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick IV–VI), common sites: ear, sternum, deltoid, jaw. Histology: thick hyalinised collagen bundles, type III > type I collagen, increased fibroblast activity, TGF-β driven. Recurrence after excision alone is very high (~45–100%) — requires adjuvant therapy (intralesional triamcinolone, silicone sheets, radiation). Hypertrophic scar: stays WITHIN wound margins, may regress over 12–18 months, less collagen disorganisation. Both have increased TGF-β signalling but keloid has persistent dysregulated fibroblast activity. Option C is reversed — keloid has type III > type I.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Necrosis — Types and Pathological Basis
questions.question_text: Coagulative necrosis is seen in all of the following EXCEPT?

options.A: Myocardial infarction
options.B: Renal infarction
options.C: Brain infarction
options.D: Splenic infarction

questions.explanation: Brain infarction produces LIQUEFACTIVE necrosis — not coagulative. The brain is rich in phospholipids and hydrolytic enzymes (phospholipases), has a high water content, and lacks a rigid stromal framework. Ischaemic neurons release proteolytic enzymes → rapid liquefaction → cystic cavity. Coagulative necrosis: ischaemia in all solid organs EXCEPT the brain (protein denaturation > enzymatic digestion → ghost cell outlines preserved on H&E for days). TB lung → caseous necrosis (cheese-like, combination of coagulative + liquefactive). Fat necrosis: pancreas (enzymatic — lipase), breast (traumatic). Fibrinoid necrosis: vessel walls in hypertension, immune complex disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Cell Biology — Labile, Stable, Permanent Cells
questions.question_text: Which of the following CORRECTLY pairs cell types with their proliferative capacity category?

options.A: Neurons — Labile; Hepatocytes — Stable; Intestinal epithelium — Permanent
options.B: Hepatocytes — Stable; Intestinal epithelium — Labile; Cardiac myocytes — Permanent
options.C: Cardiac myocytes — Stable; Hepatocytes — Labile; Neurons — Permanent
options.D: Skeletal muscle — Labile; Renal tubular cells — Permanent; Bone marrow — Stable

questions.explanation: Cell proliferative categories: Labile cells (continuously cycling, always in cell cycle): surface epithelia (GI, respiratory, urinary), bone marrow haematopoietic cells, skin keratinocytes. Stable cells (G0 resting, but can re-enter cell cycle upon injury): hepatocytes, renal tubular cells, pancreatic acinar cells, smooth muscle, fibroblasts, endothelium. Permanent cells (terminally differentiated, cannot divide): neurons, cardiac myocytes, skeletal muscle fibres (though satellite cells can regenerate). Clinical significance: permanent cells — injury leads to scarring/fibrosis (e.g., MI heals by scar, not myocardial regeneration). Stable cells — liver can regenerate after partial hepatectomy (up to 75% removal). Option A: intestinal epithelium is labile, neurons are permanent — incorrectly placed. Option C: hepatocytes are stable, not labile.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Apoptosis — Morphology and Mechanism
questions.question_text: A pathologist examining a liver biopsy from a patient with viral hepatitis notes scattered single acidophilic (eosinophilic) round bodies with condensed nuclear material and intact membranes, without surrounding inflammation. Which of the following statements about these bodies is MOST accurate?

options.A: These are Councilman bodies (apoptotic bodies) — they arise from necrosis, trigger inflammation, and represent caspase-independent cell death
options.B: These are Councilman bodies (apoptotic bodies) — they represent caspase-mediated programmed cell death with cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis), and membrane-bound fragments that are phagocytosed without triggering inflammation
options.C: These bodies arise from oncotic (necrotic) cell swelling and represent the end stage of cell membrane rupture
options.D: These are Mallory-Denk bodies (alcoholic hyaline) representing intermediate filament aggregates specific to viral hepatitis

questions.explanation: Councilman/Acidophil bodies in viral hepatitis = apoptotic bodies. Apoptosis morphology: cell shrinkage + cytoplasmic condensation → chromatin condensation at nuclear periphery (pyknosis) → nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis) → membrane blebbing → pinch off into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies → phagocytosed by macrophages/adjacent cells → NO inflammation (membranes intact, no DAMPs released). Caspase cascade: Intrinsic pathway (mitochondrial) — Bax/Bak pores → cytochrome c → apoptosome → caspase 9 → caspase 3. Extrinsic pathway (death receptor) — FasL/TNF → FADD → caspase 8 → caspase 3. BCL-2 is anti-apoptotic (inhibits cytochrome c release). Contrast with necrosis: cell swelling, membrane rupture, release of intracellular contents (DAMPs) → inflammation. Mallory-Denk bodies (option D) = keratin 8/18 intermediate filament aggregates seen in alcoholic hepatitis, NASH — not viral hepatitis specifically.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Barrett's Oesophagus — Metaplasia, Risk and Surveillance
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old obese man with a 15-year history of heartburn undergoes upper GI endoscopy which shows salmon-coloured mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Which of the following statements about this condition is MOST accurate?

options.A: This represents squamous to transitional metaplasia; risk of squamous cell carcinoma is the main concern; no surveillance is required if symptoms are controlled with PPI
options.B: This is Barrett's oesophagus — intestinal metaplasia (specialised columnar epithelium with goblet cells) replacing normal stratified squamous epithelium due to chronic GORD; goblet cells (alcian blue+, pH 2.5) are the defining histological feature; the principal cancer risk is oesophageal ADENOCARCINOMA (not SCC); surveillance endoscopy with systematic 4-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm (Seattle protocol) is recommended
options.C: This is gastric metaplasia of the oesophagus; goblet cells are not required for diagnosis; it carries the same cancer risk as squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus
options.D: Barrett's oesophagus is defined by cardiac-type columnar epithelium WITHOUT goblet cells; the cancer sequence is Barrett's → low grade dysplasia → squamous cell carcinoma

questions.explanation: Barrett's oesophagus: chronic GORD → acid/bile reflux injury → normal stratified squamous epithelium of lower oesophagus replaced by specialised intestinal metaplasia (columnar epithelium with goblet cells = alcian blue-positive mucin at pH 2.5). Goblet cells are the sine qua non — their presence distinguishes true Barrett's from cardiac metaplasia (which lacks goblet cells and carries less cancer risk in most guidelines, though UK/European guidelines accept any columnar metaplasia). Length: short-segment (<3 cm), long-segment (≥3 cm — higher cancer risk). Cancer sequence: Barrett's → low-grade dysplasia (LGD) → high-grade dysplasia (HGD) → oesophageal ADENOCARCINOMA (lower third/GOJ). Annual risk of adenocarcinoma: ~0.1–0.3% per year in Barrett's without dysplasia; 6–19% per year in HGD. Molecular progression: p16 loss → TP53 mutation → aneuploidy. Management: PPI (symptom control, slows progression); surveillance per Seattle protocol (4-quadrant biopsies every 1–2 cm); HGD → endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) + radiofrequency ablation (RFA).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Granulomatous Inflammation — Types and Diseases
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and raised serum ACE. Biopsy of a lymph node shows compact aggregates of epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, and a rim of lymphocytes WITHOUT central caseation. Which of the following BEST explains why these granulomas lack caseation, and which additional feature would shift the diagnosis toward tuberculosis?

options.A: Absence of caseation indicates a fungal aetiology; AFB staining would confirm TB if positive
options.B: Non-caseating granulomas are characteristic of sarcoidosis (type IV/delayed hypersensitivity to unknown antigen — possibly mycobacterial cell wall components); caseation occurs in TB due to cell-mediated immunity causing central necrosis (liquefactive-coagulative) from activated macrophage cytotoxicity and TNF-α — presence of central caseous necrosis, AFB on ZN stain, and positive culture would shift diagnosis to TB
options.C: Non-caseating granulomas are pathognomonic of Crohn's disease; elevated ACE and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy are also seen in Crohn's
options.D: Caseation is determined by the number of Langhans giant cells; more than 5 giant cells per granuloma confirms TB regardless of necrosis

questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis: systemic granulomatous disease of unknown aetiology — likely aberrant type IV (CD4+ Th1-mediated) hypersensitivity response to poorly degradable antigens (possibly mycobacterial, propionibacterial antigens). Non-caseating granulomas (compact epithelioid cells + Langhans/foreign body giant cells + lymphocytic rim, NO central necrosis). Special features in sarcoid granulomas: Schaumann bodies (calcium-protein concentric lamellations) and asteroid bodies (stellate inclusions in giant cells). ACE elevated (produced by epithelioid macrophages). TB granulomas: CASEATING — central caseous necrosis (cheese-like, pale eosinophilic) due to: (1) TNF-α from activated macrophages causing direct necrosis, (2) ischaemia, (3) cell-mediated cytotoxicity. ZN stain: AFB (red rods on blue background). Granulomatous inflammation causes: Caseating — TB, histoplasma, coccidioidomycosis, leprosy (tuberculoid). Non-caseating — sarcoidosis, Crohn's, berylliosis, foreign body, Wegener's (now GPA), primary biliary cirrhosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Vasculitis — Classification and PAN
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old HBsAg-positive man presents with fever, weight loss, mononeuritis multiplex, hypertension, and tender nodules along the course of small arteries. Renal angiography shows multiple microaneurysms. Skin biopsy shows segmental fibrinoid necrosis of a medium-sized muscular artery with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate and no granuloma formation. ANCA is negative. Which of the following is the MOST accurate statement about this condition?

options.A: This is Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA); c-ANCA (PR3) is the diagnostic marker; lung and kidney are the primary targets
options.B: This is Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN): medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis involving medium-sized muscular arteries; classically SPARES the pulmonary arteries and SPARES capillaries/venules; HBV association in ~30% (immune complex-mediated); p-ANCA negative; microaneurysms on angiography are characteristic; mononeuritis multiplex from vasa nervorum involvement; treatment: cyclophosphamide + corticosteroids (antiviral therapy for HBV-associated PAN)
options.C: This is microscopic polyangiitis (MPA): small vessel vasculitis, p-ANCA positive (MPO), affects pulmonary capillaries causing pulmonary haemorrhage
options.D: This is Kawasaki disease: medium vessel vasculitis in adults, HBV-associated, causing coronary artery aneurysms

questions.explanation: PAN (Polyarteritis Nodosa): medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis. Key distinguishing features: (1) Medium muscular arteries only — NOT capillaries, venules, or arterioles (unlike MPA/GPA). (2) SPARES pulmonary arteries (unlike MPA) — NO pulmonary haemorrhage. (3) ANCA NEGATIVE (unlike MPA/GPA). (4) HBV association (~30%) — hepatitis B surface antigen → immune complex deposition in vessel walls → complement activation → fibrinoid necrosis. (5) Segmental lesions — all stages simultaneously (acute, healing, healed). (6) Microaneurysms on renal/mesenteric angiography (due to weakened vessel wall). Clinical: mononeuritis multiplex (vasa nervorum), hypertension (renal artery involvement → renin), abdominal angina (mesenteric), testicular pain (testicular artery). Histology: transmural fibrinoid necrosis + mixed PMN/mononuclear infiltrate, NO granulomas, NO giant cells. Treatment: HBV-PAN — antivirals (tenofovir) + short-course steroids + plasma exchange; non-HBV PAN — cyclophosphamide + corticosteroids. MPA (option C): small vessel ANCA-positive (MPO/p-ANCA), pulmonary-renal syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Psammoma Bodies — Tumours and Pathogenesis
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman undergoes thyroidectomy for a thyroid nodule. Histology shows a papillary tumour with ground glass 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei, nuclear grooves, intranuclear pseudoinclusions, and concentric calcified lamellated structures within the papillae. Which of the following BEST explains the pathogenesis of these calcified structures AND identifies the tumour in which they are LEAST likely to be found?

options.A: These are Schaumann bodies formed by calcium-protein deposition in giant cells; least likely in serous ovarian carcinoma
options.B: These are Psammoma bodies — concentric calcified lamellations formed by dystrophic calcification around necrotic tumour cells or by mineralisation of papillary fronds; found in papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary, meningioma, and papillary renal cell carcinoma; LEAST likely in mucinous tumours (mucinous adenocarcinoma of colon/ovary) because mucin-secreting cells do not form papillae and necrosis pattern differs
options.C: These are asteroid bodies formed by collagen deposition in sarcoid granulomas; least likely in meningioma
options.D: Psammoma bodies are pathognomonic of papillary thyroid carcinoma only and are not found in any other tumour type

questions.explanation: Psammoma bodies: concentrically laminated calcified structures formed by: (1) dystrophic calcification of necrotic tumour cell clusters within papillary fronds, OR (2) mineralisation of hyalinised stroma in papillary tumours. They are calcospherites — calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate deposited in concentric rings. Tumours associated with psammoma bodies (mnemonic MOPS): Meningioma, Ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma, Papillary thyroid carcinoma, Serous papillary carcinoma of endometrium, papillary renal cell carcinoma. Also: mesothelioma. NOT found in: mucinous tumours (mucinous cystadenocarcinoma ovary, mucinous adenocarcinoma colon) — these are non-papillary, mucin-secreting, and necrosis pattern does not favour psammoma body formation. This case = Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC): 'Orphan Annie eye' nuclei (cleared/empty nuclei), nuclear grooves, intranuclear pseudoinclusions (cytoplasmic invaginations), psammoma bodies. Most common thyroid malignancy (~80%). BRAF V600E mutation in ~60%. Excellent prognosis. RET/PTC rearrangements in radiation-induced PTC.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Fibrinoid Necrosis — Pathogenesis and Diseases
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman with SLE presents with rapidly progressive renal failure. Renal biopsy shows eosinophilic, homogeneous, refractile deposits in arteriolar walls staining positively for fibrin and IgG on immunofluorescence. Which of the following BEST explains the pathogenesis of this finding and names all major conditions in which it is seen?

options.A: Caseous necrosis of arteriolar walls from granulomatous inflammation; seen in TB, sarcoidosis, and Crohn's disease
options.B: Fibrinoid necrosis: deposition of plasma proteins (including fibrin, complement, immunoglobulins) in vessel walls, combined with coagulative necrosis of the media; seen in — (1) Malignant hypertension (hyaline arteriolosclerosis → fibrinoid necrosis at very high pressures), (2) Immune complex vasculitis: SLE, PAN, serum sickness — immune complexes activate complement → C3a/C5a attract neutrophils → degranulation → protease/ROS-mediated vessel wall destruction → fibrin leakage into wall, (3) Rheumatic fever (Aschoff nodule vessels), (4) Wegener's/GPA (granulomatous vasculitis)
options.C: Fibrinoid necrosis is a variant of coagulative necrosis caused by ischaemia and is pathognomonic of myocardial infarction
options.D: Amyloid deposition in arteriolar walls staining with Congo red; seen in multiple myeloma and AL amyloidosis

questions.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis: distinctive form of necrosis seen in vessel walls — NOT simply coagulative necrosis of parenchyma. Mechanism: (1) In immune complex disease (SLE, PAN, serum sickness): type III hypersensitivity → immune complex deposition in vessel walls → complement activation → neutrophil recruitment → release of proteases (elastase, collagenase) and ROS → wall destruction → plasma protein leak into wall including fibrinogen → deposited as fibrin → eosinophilic homogeneous fibrinoid appearance on H&E. (2) In malignant hypertension: extreme pressure → endothelial injury → insudation of plasma proteins including fibrin into wall. Staining: eosinophilic/pink on H&E, PTAH or Masson trichrome confirms fibrin, immunofluorescence shows IgG, C3 in immune complex disease. Conditions: malignant hypertension, SLE nephritis, PAN, serum sickness, rheumatic fever (vessels of Aschoff nodules), scleroderma, ANCA vasculitis. Rheumatic fever: Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic — Aschoff cells (modified macrophages with 'caterpillar/owl eye' nuclei) + fibrinoid necrosis of collagen + Anitschkow cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Takayasu Arteritis — Pathology and Clinical Features
questions.question_text: A 24-year-old Asian woman presents with left arm claudication, absent left radial pulse, blood pressure differential >20 mmHg between arms, and elevated ESR. Aortography shows narrowing of the left subclavian and left common carotid arteries. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells involving the adventitia and media of the aorta. Which statement about this condition's pathology and management is MOST accurate?

options.A: This is Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA/temporal arteritis): affects patients >50 years, involves temporal and ophthalmic arteries, treated with high-dose prednisolone; temporal artery biopsy is diagnostic
options.B: This is Takayasu arteritis ('pulseless disease'): large vessel granulomatous vasculitis predominantly affecting the aorta and its major branches in young Asian women (<40 years); pathology — transmural granulomatous inflammation (adventitia → media → intima) → intimal fibrosis → luminal narrowing → arm/leg claudication, absent pulses, BP differential; complications: HTN (renal artery stenosis), visual loss (carotid/ophthalmic), aortic regurgitation; management: high-dose corticosteroids (first-line); refractory cases: methotrexate, azathioprine, tocilizumab (IL-6 inhibitor); revascularisation when disease quiescent
options.C: This is Kawasaki disease: medium vessel vasculitis in young children involving coronary arteries; treated with IV immunoglobulin and aspirin
options.D: This is Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans): small-medium vessel inflammatory thrombosis in young male smokers; treated with smoking cessation

questions.explanation: Takayasu arteritis: large vessel vasculitis (aorta + major branches). Demographics: Asian women <40 years (mean age 25). Pathology: CD4+ T-cell and NK cell-mediated granulomatous inflammation of vessel wall → starts in adventitia → media → intima → fibrosis → stenosis. 'Skip lesions' possible. Pathological stages: (1) Early (systemic): fever, elevated ESR, CRP; (2) Late (occlusive/pulseless): absent pulses, bruits, BP differential. Blood supply territories affected: subclavian (arm claudication, absent pulse), carotid (visual symptoms, syncope, stroke), renal arteries (renovascular HTN — most common cause of HTN in young women in Asia), aortic arch (aortic regurgitation). Differentiation from GCA: GCA — age >50, temporal artery, jaw claudication, risk of sudden blindness (anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy), ESR >50, responds to prednisolone; temporal artery biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with fragmentation of internal elastic lamina. Both: large vessel vasculitis, granulomatous, steroid-responsive.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Giant Cell Tumour of Bone — Pathology and Imaging
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents with chronic knee pain and swelling. X-ray of the distal femur shows an eccentric, lytic lesion with a 'soap bubble' appearance extending to the articular surface, with no periosteal reaction and no calcification. Histology shows a dual population of mononuclear stromal cells (RANKL-expressing) and evenly distributed osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells. Which of the following is the MOST accurate statement about the molecular pathology, clinical behaviour, and targeted therapy of this tumour?

options.A: This is osteosarcoma; the mononuclear cells produce alkaline phosphatase (ALP); osteoid matrix is produced; treated with neoadjuvant methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin
options.B: This is Giant Cell Tumour of Bone (GCTB): the pathological cells are the RANKL-expressing mononuclear stromal cells (neoplastic component), not the giant cells; giant cells are recruited osteoclast precursors activated by RANKL-RANK signalling and cause bone resorption; driver mutation: H3.3 histone gene (H3F3A) mutation (G34W/L) in stromal cells; denosumab (anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody) inhibits giant cell-mediated bone destruction — used in unresectable/recurrent GCTB; ~5% undergo malignant transformation
options.C: This is aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC); the lesion is entirely haemorrhagic with blood-filled spaces; H3F3A mutation is absent; treated with curettage only
options.D: This is chondroblastoma; it arises from the epiphysis in young patients, shows 'chicken-wire' calcification pattern, and is treated with radiofrequency ablation

questions.explanation: Giant Cell Tumour of Bone (GCTB / Osteoclastoma): Location — EPIPHYSIS of long bones after growth plate closure (distal femur most common, then proximal tibia, distal radius). Age: 20–40 years. X-ray: eccentric, lytic, 'soap bubble', extends to subchondral bone, NO matrix mineralisation. Pathology: dual population — (1) mononuclear spindle stromal cells = TRUE neoplastic cells; (2) osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells = reactive osteoclast precursors recruited by RANKL expressed on stromal cells → RANK-RANKL binding → osteoclast activation → bone resorption. Molecular: H3F3A (H3.3 histone) mutation — G34W (most common) or G34L — detectable by IHC with anti-H3.3 G34W antibody. Behaviour: locally aggressive (Campanacci grade I–III), ~2% metastasise to lung (even histologically benign). Malignant GCT (~5%): primary or secondary (post-radiation). Treatment: curettage + bone cement/graft (local recurrence ~20%); denosumab (anti-RANKL) for unresectable cases — inhibits osteoclast recruitment → reduces giant cells → fills lesion with bone; pre-operative denosumab before difficult resections. Differential: chondroblastoma (epiphysis, younger patients, 'chicken-wire' calcification, S100+, H3F3B K36M mutation), ABC (secondary to GCT in 20%, blood-filled cavities).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Dermatomyositis — Pathology and Malignancy Association
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, raising arms), a heliotrope rash around the eyes, Gottron's papules over the knuckles, and elevated CK (3,200 U/L). EMG shows myopathic changes. Muscle biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy and perivascular B-cell and CD4+ T-cell infiltrates. Which of the following is the MOST accurate statement about the immunopathogenesis and the most important systemic association to investigate?

options.A: This is polymyositis: cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells directly invade and destroy individual muscle fibres (endomysial infiltrate); anti-Jo-1 antibody is pathognomonic; no malignancy association
options.B: This is dermatomyositis: humorally-mediated complement-dependent microangiopathy — complement (MAC/C5b-9) deposits on endomysial capillaries → capillary destruction → perifascicular ischaemia → perifascicular atrophy; mediated by plasmacytoid dendritic cells and type I interferon pathway; anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-γ (most strongly associated with malignancy), anti-MDA5 antibodies; malignancy (occult cancer) must be actively excluded — occurs in ~15–30% of adult dermatomyositis, most commonly ovarian, lung, GI, breast, nasopharyngeal cancers; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + age-appropriate cancer screening mandatory
options.C: This is inclusion body myositis (IBM): most common inflammatory myopathy in patients >50 years; distal + proximal weakness (finger flexors + knee extensors); rimmed vacuoles on biopsy; anti-cN-1A antibody; no malignancy association; does not respond to steroids
options.D: This is amyopathic dermatomyositis: skin rash without muscle weakness; no CK elevation; no malignancy risk; treated with topical steroids only

questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis (DM): immune-mediated myopathy. Immunopathogenesis: Type I interferon-driven humoral process — plasmacytoid dendritic cells in muscle → IFN-α production → B-cell and CD4+ T-cell perivascular infiltrates → complement activation → MAC (C5b-9) deposits on endomysial capillaries → microangiopathy → perifascicular ischaemia → perifascicular atrophy (pathognomonic on muscle biopsy). Compare with Polymyositis (PM): CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells directly invade non-necrotic muscle fibres (endomysial infiltrate) → MHC-I upregulation on fibres. DM-specific antibodies: anti-Mi-2 (classic DM, good prognosis), anti-TIF1-γ/anti-p155/140 (MOST strongly associated with malignancy — especially in older adults), anti-MDA5 (rapidly progressive ILD, amyopathic DM, skin ulcers), anti-NXP-2 (calcinosis in juvenile DM). Malignancy association: DM >PM >IBM (IBM = none). Risk: 15–30% of adult DM. Timing: can precede, coincide, or follow cancer diagnosis. Commonest associated cancers: ovarian (most common in women), lung, colorectal, breast, nasopharynx. IBM (option C): steroid-resistant, asymmetric distal+proximal, rimmed vacuoles + 15–18 nm filamentous inclusions on EM.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Pulmonary Embolism — Pathology and Virchow's Triad
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man who had a right total knee replacement 10 days ago develops sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, and haemoptysis. His SpO2 is 88%. CT pulmonary angiography confirms bilateral pulmonary emboli. Autopsy of a similar fatal case would show haemorrhagic infarction of which lung zone, and which component of Virchow's triad is MOST relevant here?

options.A: Upper lobe infarction; endothelial injury from surgical trauma is the primary mechanism; lungs have no dual blood supply
options.B: Pulmonary infarction preferentially involves the lower lobes (most blood flow) and is typically haemorrhagic (red infarct) because the lung has a DUAL blood supply — pulmonary artery + bronchial artery; infarction only occurs when bronchial collateral flow is ALSO compromised (e.g., pre-existing cardiopulmonary disease); in this case, hypercoagulability (post-surgical) and stasis (immobilisation post-knee surgery) are the two most relevant arms of Virchow's triad
options.C: Pulmonary infarction always produces white (anaemic) infarction as the lung parenchyma is avascular; Virchow's triad: endothelial injury from the surgical incision is the primary mechanism
options.D: PE never causes infarction because the bronchial circulation always compensates; the only consequence is pulmonary hypertension

questions.explanation: Pulmonary Embolism — pathological anatomy: Emboli typically arise from DVT of deep leg veins (popliteal, femoral, iliac — > 90%). Post-orthopaedic surgery (hip/knee replacement) is among the highest DVT/PE risk procedures. Virchow's triad: (1) Stasis — immobilisation post-surgery, (2) Hypercoagulability — surgical trauma triggers coagulation cascade, tissue factor release, platelet activation; also post-operative acute phase reaction. (3) Endothelial injury — less dominant here (surgical vein injury contributes to DVT initiation). Pulmonary infarction: occurs in only ~10% of PE (lungs have dual circulation: pulmonary artery + bronchial artery). Infarction occurs when: (1) Peripheral emboli (segmental/subsegmental arteries) where collaterals insufficient, AND (2) Pre-existing compromised bronchial circulation (cardiac failure, pre-existing lung disease). Morphology: haemorrhagic (red) infarct — lung capillaries (from bronchial artery) engorge with blood into necrotic area; wedge-shaped, pleura-based, lower lobe (most blood flow). Histology: coagulative necrosis of alveolar walls + intra-alveolar haemorrhage. Clinically: Hampton's hump on CXR (peripheral wedge opacity), Westermark sign (oligaemia). Treatment: anticoagulation (LMWH/DOAC); massive PE with haemodynamic compromise: systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) or catheter-directed therapy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Pancreatitis — Pathology and Complications
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, and abdominal rigidity. Serum lipase is 1,800 U/L (normal <60). CT abdomen shows peripancreatic fat stranding, necrotic areas within the pancreas, and a fluid collection. Which of the following MOST accurately explains the pathological mechanism of fat necrosis in the peripancreatic tissue AND the cause of hypocalcaemia in this patient?

options.A: Fat necrosis occurs due to direct pressure necrosis from the inflamed pancreas; hypocalcaemia is from SIADH causing dilutional hyponatraemia and hypocalcaemia
options.B: Enzymatic fat necrosis: activated pancreatic lipase released from acinar cells hydrolyses triglycerides in peripancreatic adipocytes → free fatty acids (FFAs) + glycerol; FFAs combine with calcium ions → calcium soaps (saponification) → chalky white deposits (fat necrosis) on gross examination; hypocalcaemia results from calcium sequestration in these saponification deposits (calcium soaps); additionally, glucagon release → calcitonin release → hypocalcaemia; tetany if Ca²⁺ <7 mg/dL; hypocalcaemia is a marker of severity (Ranson's criterion)
options.C: Fat necrosis in pancreatitis is due to traumatic rupture of adipocytes by the inflammatory exudate, not enzyme action; hypocalcaemia is due to hypoalbuminaemia causing a decrease in protein-bound calcium only, with normal ionised calcium
options.D: The chalky white deposits represent dystrophic calcification of necrotic acinar cells, not fat necrosis; calcium deposits in dying cells from calcium influx during necrosis

questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis — fat necrosis mechanism: Acinar cell injury (alcohol, gallstone) → premature intracellular activation of trypsinogen → trypsin → activates lipase, elastase, phospholipase A2. Activated lipase released into peripancreatic tissue → hydrolyses adipocyte triglycerides → FFAs + glycerol. FFAs + Ca²⁺ → calcium soaps (saponification) → chalk-white, opaque deposits (ghosts of fat cells with shadowy outlines, surrounded by saponified material on H&E). Hypocalcaemia: (1) PRIMARY mechanism — saponification sequesters large amounts of Ca²⁺ from circulation; (2) Glucagon released → stimulates calcitonin → ↓serum calcium; (3) Hypoalbuminaemia (from capillary leak, third spacing) reduces protein-bound calcium. Severity markers — Ranson's criteria include: hypocalcaemia <8 mg/dL at 48h (poor prognosis marker); serum Ca²⁺ <7 → tetany risk. Complications: (1) Acute — SIRS/sepsis, ARDS (phospholipase A2 destroys surfactant), AKI, DIC, bleeding; (2) Early local — acute peripancreatic fluid collection, acute necrotic collection; (3) Late — pseudocyst (4+ weeks, walled-off fluid collection lined by fibrous tissue, NOT true epithelial lining), walled-off necrosis (WON). Chronic pancreatitis: dystrophic calcification, pancreatic duct dilation, exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhoea), endocrine insufficiency (diabetes).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Lung Carcinoma — Pathological Types and Paraneoplastic Syndromes
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male smoker presents with haemoptysis, 10 kg weight loss, and confusion. CT shows a central hilar mass. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L (hyponatraemia). The bronchoscopy biopsy image above shows sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear moulding, crush artefact, and 'salt and pepper' chromatin on H&E. IHC: synaptophysin+, chromogranin+, CD56+, TTF-1+, CK (dot-like)+, Ki-67 >80%. Which of the following MOST accurately identifies the tumour, its paraneoplastic syndrome mechanism, and its relationship to smoking?

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma; paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia from PTHrP secretion; strong smoking association; central location; treated with surgery
options.B: Small Cell Lung Carcinoma (SCLC): neuroendocrine tumour of Kulchitsky cells (APUD cells) of bronchial mucosa; strong smoking association (>95%); central location; IHC: neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin, CD56) + TTF-1 (60–70%); paraneoplastic SIADH from ectopic ADH (AVP) secretion by tumour → hyponatraemia; other paraneoplastic syndromes: ectopic ACTH (Cushing's), Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (anti-VGCC antibodies), encephalomyelitis (anti-Hu/ANNA-1); treated with chemotherapy (etoposide + cisplatin/carboplatin) + immunotherapy (atezolizumab); surgery NOT standard (almost always disseminated at diagnosis)
options.C: Carcinoid tumour; low Ki-67 (<20%), no association with smoking; treated with somatostatin analogues; paraneoplastic carcinoid syndrome from serotonin
options.D: Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC); large cells with prominent nucleoli; Ki-67 20–40%; treated identically to adenocarcinoma

questions.explanation: Small Cell Lung Carcinoma (SCLC): High-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma. Origin: Kulchitsky (neuroendocrine) cells of bronchial epithelium. Morphology: Small cells (2× lymphocyte size), scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic 'salt and pepper' chromatin, nuclear moulding (cells mould to each other), prominent crush artefact (fragile cells), geographic necrosis, Azzopardi effect (basophilic encrustation of vessel walls with DNA). IHC: CD56, synaptophysin, chromogranin A (neuroendocrine), TTF-1+, CK (dot-like paranuclear pattern), Ki-67 >70–80%. Paraneoplastic syndromes (SCLC most common cause of all paraneoplastic syndromes): (1) SIADH (most common in SCLC) → ectopic ADH/AVP → water retention → dilutional hyponatraemia (as here); (2) Ectopic ACTH → Cushing's syndrome (truncal obesity, hypertension, hypokalemia — often without typical features due to rapid onset); (3) Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) — anti-P/Q type VGCC antibodies → impaired presynaptic ACh release → proximal weakness that IMPROVES with repeated use (unlike myasthenia gravis); (4) Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) → paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis/sensory neuropathy. Squamous cell carcinoma (option A): central, PTHrP → hypercalcaemia, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, p63+, CK5/6+, TTF-1 negative. Carcinoid (option C): Ki-67 <20% (typical), no smoking association, ZES/carcinoid syndrome. Treatment of SCLC: LD-SCLC — chemoradiation (EP + chest RT) + PCI; ED-SCLC — EP + atezolizumab/durvalumab; surgery almost never (stage I small LD-SCLC only).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Renal Pathology — Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents with puffiness of the face, massive proteinuria (5.2 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia (1.8 g/dL), hyperlipidaemia, and lipiduria. Blood pressure is normal. Renal biopsy shows normal light microscopy, no immune deposits on immunofluorescence, and diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. Which of the following MOST accurately explains the pathogenesis of proteinuria in this condition and the reason for hyperlipidaemia?

options.A: This is IgA nephropathy; mesangial IgA deposits on IF; complement-mediated destruction of GBM; hyperlipidaemia from impaired hepatic lipoprotein lipase
options.B: This is Minimal Change Disease (MCD / lipoid nephrosis / nil disease): T-cell dysfunction → circulating permeability factor (possibly CD80/B7-1 on podocytes) → loss of normal podocyte glycocalyx negative charge (heparan sulphate proteoglycans) → loss of charge-selective barrier → selective proteinuria (predominantly albumin); hyperlipidaemia: hypoalbuminaemia → reduced oncotic pressure → hepatic lipoprotein synthesis upregulated (↑LDL, VLDL, cholesterol) + reduced peripheral lipolysis (↓lipoprotein lipase activity); oval fat bodies/Maltese cross on urine microscopy; STEROID-SENSITIVE (>95% respond to prednisolone)
options.C: This is FSGS; segmental sclerosis on LM; foot process effacement is partial; treat with calcineurin inhibitors; poor response to steroids
options.D: This is membranous nephropathy; subepithelial IgG + C3 deposits (spike and dome); IF shows granular IgG; commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults; anti-PLA2R antibodies

questions.explanation: Minimal Change Disease (MCD): Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (>80%). LM: NORMAL (hence 'minimal change'). IF: NO immune deposits (unlike MPGN, membranous, IgAN). EM: diffuse (global, complete) effacement/fusion of podocyte foot processes — PATHOGNOMONIC. Pathogenesis: T-cell (Th2) dysfunction → circulating permeability factor (unclear identity; possibly soluble urokinase receptor, CD80 on podocytes) → disrupts podocyte foot process architecture and glycocalyx → loss of the charge-selective (anionic) barrier of GBM (heparan sulphate proteoglycans) → SELECTIVE proteinuria (albumin >> IgG, transferrin; selectivity index <0.1). Hyperlipidaemia mechanism: Hypoalbuminaemia (protein loss) → reduced plasma oncotic pressure → liver compensates by upregulating lipoprotein synthesis (↑LDL, ↑VLDL, ↑total cholesterol) + reduced lipoprotein lipase activity in periphery → hyperlipidaemia. Lipiduria: oval fat bodies (lipid-laden tubular epithelial cells) + free fat droplets → Maltese cross birefringence under polarised light. Treatment: prednisolone (60 mg/m²/day × 4 weeks) → >95% remission; relapses common (60%); frequent relapsers/steroid-dependent → cyclophosphamide, levamisole, mycophenolate, calcineurin inhibitors, rituximab. Prognosis: excellent in children (most outgrow disease); adults less responsive.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Aortic Dissection — Pathology and Predisposing Conditions
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old tall, thin man with arm span > height and high-arched palate presents with sudden, severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, with unequal blood pressure between arms. CT aortography shows an intimal tear at the ascending aorta with a false lumen. Which of the following MOST accurately identifies the underlying pre-existing aortic pathology, its molecular basis, and the immediate life-threatening complications?

options.A: Atherosclerosis of the descending aorta; cholesterol plaque rupture causing intimal tear; complication is peripheral vascular disease
options.B: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation, chromosome 15q): defective fibrillin-1 → abnormal microfibril scaffold → excessive TGF-β signalling (fibrillin normally sequesters TGF-β) → medial degeneration (cystic medial necrosis = loss of smooth muscle cells and elastic fibres with mucoid/myxoid pools in aortic media) → aortic root dilatation → intimal tear → Type A dissection (Stanford: ascending aorta involved); immediate life-threatening complications: (1) haemopericardium → cardiac tamponade, (2) aortic regurgitation from annular dilatation, (3) coronary artery involvement → acute MI, (4) carotid occlusion → stroke; treatment: emergency surgical repair (Type A = surgical emergency)
options.C: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Type IV (COL3A1 mutation): defective type III collagen; the primary complication is arterial aneurysm rupture, not aortic dissection; treated conservatively
options.D: Syphilitic aortitis: obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum → medial ischaemia → 'tree bark' appearance of intima; primarily involves arch aneurysm not dissection; treated with penicillin

questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome: autosomal dominant, FBN1 gene (chromosome 15q21) → defective fibrillin-1 → abnormal microfibrils in elastic tissues. Molecular mechanism: fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-β in extracellular matrix; defective fibrillin → excess free TGF-β → upregulates MMP production → elastin/collagen degradation + smooth muscle apoptosis → cystic medial necrosis (medionecrosis): (1) fragmentation/loss of elastic fibres, (2) apoptosis of medial smooth muscle cells, (3) mucoid/myxoid (proteoglycan) pools in media. This weakens the aortic wall → aortic root dilation (sinus of Valsalva) → predisposes to: (1) aortic dissection, (2) aortic regurgitation, (3) mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration). Stanford classification: Type A (ascending ± arch ± descending) — surgical emergency; Type B (descending only, distal to L subclavian) — medical management (IV beta-blockers to reduce aortic wall stress, then endovascular repair if complicated). De Bakey: I (ascending + descending), II (ascending only), III (descending only). Immediate complications of Type A: pericardial tamponade (blood in pericardium), severe AR, MI (RCA most common), stroke (carotid involvement), acute renal failure, visceral ischaemia. Treatment: Marfan — lifelong beta-blockers + ARBs (losartan reduces TGF-β signalling) + prophylactic aortic root replacement when diameter >4.5–5 cm.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Pre-eclampsia — Renal and Placental Pathology
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation presents with BP 160/110 mmHg, proteinuria (3+), headache, and oedema. Investigations: platelets 85,000/μL, ALT 180 U/L, serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Which of the following MOST accurately explains the renal pathology seen in this condition and correctly identifies the severe variant with its defining criteria?

options.A: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with immune complex deposition (wire-loop lesions); seen in pre-eclampsia; treated with high-dose steroids
options.B: Glomerular endotheliosis: the pathognomonic renal lesion of pre-eclampsia — swelling and vacuolation of glomerular endothelial cells (loss of endothelial fenestrations) → obliteration of glomerular capillary lumina → reduced GFR + proteinuria; pathogenesis: defective trophoblast invasion of spiral arteries → placental ischaemia → excess sFlt-1 (soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase-1, anti-VEGF) and reduced PlGF released → endothelial dysfunction systemically; HELLP syndrome (severe variant): Haemolysis (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia), Elevated Liver enzymes (periportal hepatic necrosis, subcapsular haematoma), Low Platelets (<100,000); treatment: delivery is definitive; antihypertensives (labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine); MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis/eclampsia
options.C: Acute tubular necrosis from hypotension is the primary renal lesion; proteinuria is from tubular dysfunction, not glomerular injury; HELLP requires platelets <50,000 for diagnosis
options.D: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) developing secondary to pre-eclampsia; requires renal biopsy for diagnosis; treated with calcineurin inhibitors post-delivery

questions.explanation: Pre-eclampsia: hypertension (≥140/90) + proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h or ≥2+ dipstick) after 20 weeks gestation in previously normotensive woman. Pathognomonic renal lesion: GLOMERULAR ENDOTHELIOSIS — swelling and vacuolation of glomerular endothelial cells → cytoplasmic protrusions obliterate capillary lumina → bloodless glomeruli on LM → ↓GFR + proteinuria. NO immune complex deposits (unlike lupus nephritis). Pathogenesis: Shallow trophoblast invasion of decidual (not myometrial) spiral arteries → high-resistance uteroplacental circulation → placental ischaemia → release of sFlt-1 (soluble VEGF receptor 1 — decoy receptor binding VEGF and PlGF) → systemic endothelial dysfunction → hypertension, proteinuria, cerebral oedema (eclampsia), hepatic endotheliosis. sFlt-1/PlGF ratio elevated before clinical disease. HELLP syndrome: Haemolysis (↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, schistocytes on smear), EL (ALT/AST >70 U/L; subcapsular liver haematoma risk), LP (<100,000/μL platelets → DIC risk). Diagnostic threshold: platelets <100,000 (NOT <50,000). Treatment: Definitive = DELIVERY. Antihypertensives: labetalol IV (first-line), hydralazine, oral nifedipine. MgSO4: prevents/treats eclamptic seizures (mechanism: blocks NMDA receptors, reduces cerebral vasospasm, neuroprotection). Toxicity of MgSO4: respiratory depression (antidote: calcium gluconate IV).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Cystic Fibrosis — Pathology and Pulmonary Complications
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old boy with recurrent chest infections, failure to thrive, and steatorrhoea is found to have sweat chloride of 82 mEq/L (normal <40). Sputum culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa (mucoid colony). Which of the following MOST accurately explains the molecular defect in the most common mutation, its consequence on epithelial function, and why Pseudomonas aeruginosa is particularly problematic in this condition?

options.A: CFTR ΔF508 mutation causes a Class I defect (no protein synthesis); chloride channel is absent from birth; Pseudomonas is problematic due to immunodeficiency from neutropenia
options.B: CFTR ΔF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508): Class II defect — misfolded CFTR protein retained in endoplasmic reticulum and degraded by proteasome → no CFTR reaches apical membrane of epithelial cells → absent Cl⁻ secretion + increased Na⁺ absorption → dehydrated, viscous mucus → impaired mucociliary clearance → chronic airway infection; Pseudomonas aeruginosa forms alginate-coated BIOFILMS in viscous mucus (mucoid phenotype) → protected from antibiotics and phagocytosis → chronic endobronchial infection → neutrophil-dominated inflammatory response → elastase/protease release → progressive bronchiectasis and pulmonary destruction; treatment: CFTR modulators — ivacaftor (Class III gating mutations, e.g., G551D), lumacaftor/ivacaftor or elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ΔF508)
options.C: CFTR ΔF508 is a Class V mutation (reduced CFTR synthesis); only pulmonary disease occurs; GI manifestations absent; Pseudomonas is problematic due to exotoxin A causing haemolysis
options.D: The defect is in the sodium channel ENaC (not CFTR); excess Na⁺ secretion dries the airway surface liquid; treated with amiloride inhalation alone

questions.explanation: Cystic Fibrosis: autosomal recessive, CFTR gene (chromosome 7q31). ΔF508 (delta F508) = most common mutation worldwide (~70% of CF alleles). CFTR protein classes: Class I — no protein synthesis (nonsense mutations, e.g., G542X); Class II — misfolded protein, ER retention/proteasomal degradation (ΔF508 = Class II — MOST COMMON); Class III — protein reaches membrane but gating defect (G551D — target of ivacaftor); Class IV — reduced Cl⁻ conductance; Class V — reduced synthesis; Class VI — reduced stability. Pathophysiology of ΔF508: misfolded CFTR degraded → NO apical Cl⁻ channel → (1) Airway: ↓Cl⁻ secretion + ↑ENaC Na⁺ absorption → depleted airway surface liquid (ASL) → dehydrated, sticky mucus → failure of mucociliary escalator; (2) Pancreatic ducts: inspissated secretions → obstruction → autodigestion → exocrine pancreatic insufficiency → steatorrhoea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (ADEK); (3) Vas deferens: atresia → male infertility; (4) Meconium ileus in neonates (earliest manifestation). Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm: mucoid alginate capsule in viscous mucus → impenetrable to antibiotics and neutrophils → chronic infection → neutrophil elastase/proteases → airway damage → bronchiectasis (irreversible airway dilation, cylindrical/varicose/saccular). Other organisms: early — Staph aureus; later — Pseudomonas aeruginosa (dominant); Burkholderia cepacia complex (very resistant, poor prognosis). CFTR modulators: Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta) = corrector + corrector + potentiator for ΔF508 — now standard of care, dramatically reduces lung function decline.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Wernicke's Encephalopathy — Nutritional Pathology
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with acute confusion (disorientation), bilateral lateral rectus palsy (ophthalmoplegia), and wide-based gait (ataxia). MRI brain shows T2/FLAIR hyperintensity around the mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey, and medial thalami. Which of the following MOST accurately explains the metabolic basis and neuropathological changes of this condition, and the risk of administering IV glucose before thiamine?

options.A: This is Korsakoff's psychosis; chronic irreversible condition from alcohol neurotoxicity directly; thiamine has no role; IV glucose is safe to administer
options.B: This is Wernicke's Encephalopathy (WE): thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency → deficiency of thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) — cofactor for transketolase (HMP shunt), pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (Krebs cycle) → impaired glucose oxidation and aerobic metabolism → selective neuronal injury in high metabolic demand areas (mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey, medial thalami, abducens nuclei) → petechial haemorrhages, vascular endothelial proliferation, and demyelination; administering IV glucose WITHOUT thiamine depletes residual thiamine stores → precipitates or worsens WE (glucose metabolism consumes TPP) → ALWAYS give IV thiamine (100 mg) BEFORE or WITH IV glucose in any alcoholic/malnourished patient
options.C: This is hepatic encephalopathy from alcoholic cirrhosis; ammonia accumulates → astrocyte Alzheimer type II changes; treated with lactulose and rifaximin; thiamine not relevant
options.D: This is central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination) from rapid correction of hyponatraemia; lesion is in pons not mammillary bodies; IV glucose is irrelevant

questions.explanation: Wernicke's Encephalopathy (WE): acute neurological emergency from thiamine (B1) deficiency. Classic triad: (1) Ophthalmoplegia (lateral gaze palsy/nystagmus — CN VI and CN VI nuclei in abducens), (2) Ataxia (cerebellar vermis involvement), (3) Confusion/encephalopathy. All three present in only 10–16% of cases — DO NOT wait for complete triad to treat. Metabolic basis: Thiamine → Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP): essential cofactor for (1) Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH): pyruvate → acetyl-CoA; (2) Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (Krebs cycle); (3) Transketolase (HMP shunt — pentose phosphate pathway); (4) Branched-chain amino acid decarboxylases. TPP deficiency → impaired aerobic glucose oxidation → ATP depletion → lactic acidosis → selective damage to high-metabolic-demand periventricular structures (mammillary bodies — most characteristic and earliest on MRI, periaqueductal grey, medial dorsal thalami, abducens nuclei). Neuropathology: hyperaemia, petechial haemorrhages (from endothelial injury), vascular proliferation, demyelination — then astrocytosis. Glucose before thiamine risk: glucose loading → PDH activity surge → depletes residual TPP → acute precipitation of WE in marginal thiamine stores. Treatment: THIAMINE IV 500 mg TDS for 3–5 days (Pabrinex) → then oral; BEFORE IV dextrose in any suspected nutritional deficiency. If untreated WE → Korsakoff's syndrome (permanent amnestic disorder): anterograde > retrograde amnesia + confabulation; mammillary body atrophy + mediodorsal thalamic atrophy; only ~20% recover with treatment.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Septic Shock — Pathophysiology and Organ Injury
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old diabetic man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with fever (39.8°C), hypotension (BP 80/50 mmHg), tachycardia (126/min), tachypnoea, and altered sensorium. Blood cultures grow E. coli. Despite 30 mL/kg IV fluid resuscitation, his BP remains 75/50 mmHg, lactate is 6.2 mmol/L, and he requires vasopressors. He subsequently develops bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (ARDS) and oliguria. Which of the following MOST comprehensively explains the sequence of pathological events from bacteraemia to multi-organ dysfunction in this patient?

options.A: LPS from E. coli activates complement only (C3a, C5a) → mast cell degranulation → histamine release → vasodilation and hypotension; organ failure from direct bacterial toxin-mediated necrosis; treated with antihistamines
options.B: E. coli LPS (lipopolysaccharide/endotoxin) binds TLR4-MD-2-CD14 complex on macrophages/monocytes → NF-κB activation → massive cytokine storm (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12) → (1) Vasodilation: iNOS upregulation → excess NO → ↓SVR → distributive shock; (2) Endothelial activation: E-selectin, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 upregulation → neutrophil adhesion/transmigration → ROS + elastase → endothelial injury → capillary leak; (3) Coagulation: tissue factor expression → DIC (microthrombi in glomeruli, hepatic sinusoids, adrenal cortex); (4) ARDS: neutrophil-mediated alveolar capillary injury → DAD (diffuse alveolar damage); (5) Acute tubular necrosis: ischaemia + direct cytokine-mediated tubular injury; (6) Waterhouse-Friderichsen if adrenal cortex infarction (meningococcal sepsis classically); treatment: vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line), broad-spectrum antibiotics, source control, lung-protective ventilation
options.C: Gram-positive bacteria cause more severe septic shock than gram-negative; E. coli releases exotoxins (not endotoxins) that directly lyse neutrophils; organ failure is from immune complex deposition
options.D: Septic shock is a distributive shock with increased cardiac output and decreased SVR but no endothelial injury; ARDS is unrelated to sepsis in this case; DIC does not occur in gram-negative sepsis

questions.explanation: Septic shock — complete pathophysiological cascade: E. coli = gram-negative bacteria → LPS (lipopolysaccharide) = endotoxin (lipid A is active moiety) → binds LPS-binding protein (LBP) in plasma → LBP-LPS complex → CD14 (monocyte surface) → TLR4-MD-2 intracellular signalling → MyD88 → IRAK/TRAF6 → NF-κB → transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Cytokine storm: TNF-α (cachexia, fever, shock), IL-1β (fever, endothelial activation), IL-6 (acute phase proteins), IL-8 (neutrophil chemotaxis), IL-12 (Th1 skewing). Multi-organ failure sequence: (1) Cardiovascular: NO → guanylyl cyclase → cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation → ↓SVR → distributive (warm) shock; initial ↑CO (hyperdynamic phase), myocardial depression from TNF-α/IL-1β → cardiogenic component later; (2) Lung (ARDS): neutrophil margination in alveolar capillaries → ROS, elastase → DAD phase — exudative (alveolar flooding, hyaline membranes), proliferative (type II pneumocyte hyperplasia), fibrotic; (3) Kidney (AKI): renal cortical ischaemia (vasoconstriction from catecholamines, ↓effective circulating volume) → ATN; direct cytokine-mediated tubular injury; (4) DIC: TF expression on endothelium + monocytes → thrombin generation → fibrin microthrombi; consumes clotting factors + platelets → paradoxical bleeding; D-dimer ↑, fibrinogen ↓, PT/APTT prolonged; (5) Liver: hepatic sinusoidal neutrophil trapping → hepatocyte ischaemia/cytokine injury → ↑transaminases, ↑bilirubin; (6) Adrenal (in meningococcal sepsis — Waterhouse-Friderichsen): bilateral adrenal cortical haemorrhagic infarction from DIC → acute adrenal insufficiency. Septic shock definition (Sepsis-3): sepsis + vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Management: Hour-1 bundle — blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressor (noradrenaline) if persistent hypotension, lactate measurement; hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV if refractory to vasopressors.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Hepatocellular Carcinoma — Molecular Pathogenesis and Surveillance
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man with HBV-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B) presents with rapidly worsening abdominal pain and a 4 kg weight gain over 3 weeks. AFP is 18,000 ng/mL. CT abdomen shows a 7 cm arterially enhancing lesion with washout in the right lobe of liver with portal vein tumour thrombus. The liver biopsy image above shows polygonal tumour cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, trabecular growth pattern, and a sinusoidal vascular network. Which of the following MOST accurately describes the molecular carcinogenesis of HBV-related HCC and the first-line systemic therapy?

options.A: HBV causes HCC only through cirrhosis-related regenerative nodule dysplasia; direct oncogenic effect of HBV DNA is absent; sorafenib is the only approved systemic therapy
options.B: HBV-related HCC: (1) DIRECT oncogenic mechanism — HBV DNA integrates into host hepatocyte genome (preferentially near TP53, TERT promoter, CCND1 loci) → insertional mutagenesis + chromosomal instability; HBx protein activates NF-κB, MAPK, PI3K/AKT, Wnt/β-catenin pathways; HBx suppresses TP53 tumour suppressor function; (2) INDIRECT mechanism — HBsAg-driven immune-mediated chronic hepatocyte necrosis/regeneration → cirrhosis → regenerative nodule → dysplastic nodule → HCC; TERT promoter mutation most common somatic mutation in HCC; systemic therapy for advanced HCC: first-line — atezolizumab + bevacizumab (IMbrave150 trial: superior OS/PFS vs sorafenib); sorafenib/lenvatinib alternative first-line; second-line: regorafenib, cabozantinib, ramucirumab (AFP >400)
options.C: HCV causes HCC through direct viral cytopathic effect and does not cause cirrhosis; HBV has no direct oncogenic role; first-line treatment is surgical resection for all HCC
options.D: TERT promoter mutation is absent in HCC; Wnt/β-catenin pathway is not involved; first-line systemic therapy for advanced HCC is oxaliplatin-based FOLFOX chemotherapy

questions.explanation: HBV-related HCC — dual carcinogenesis: (1) DIRECT (unique to HBV among hepatitis viruses): HBV partially double-stranded DNA integrates into hepatocyte genome (during repair of covalently closed circular DNA — cccDNA) → insertional mutagenesis (insertions near TERT promoter, MLL4, CCNE1, CCND1, FGF19) → chromosomal instability, amplifications, deletions. HBx protein (X protein): transactivates oncogenes (Myc, ras), inhibits TP53 (direct binding + ubiquitin pathway), activates survival pathways (NF-κB, MAPK, PI3K/AKT, Src). HCC can develop WITHOUT cirrhosis in HBV (unique among viral hepatitides). (2) INDIRECT: HBsAg → immune-mediated hepatocyte destruction → chronic inflammation (TNF-α, IL-6, ROS) → repeated cycles of necrosis + regeneration → regenerative nodule → low-grade dysplastic nodule → high-grade dysplastic nodule → early HCC → progressed HCC. Molecular landscape of HCC: TERT promoter mutation (most frequent, 55–60%), TP53 mutations (20–25%, enriched in HBV-HCC), CTNNB1 (β-catenin, Wnt pathway, 25–30%, enriched in HCV/alcohol-HCC), ARID1A, ARID2 (chromatin remodelling). AFP: sensitivity ~60% for HCC; specificity limited; AFP-L3 fraction more specific. CT hallmark: arterial hypervascularisation (hepatic artery supply) + venous/delayed washout = Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) 5. Systemic therapy: Advanced HCC (unresectable/metastatic): First-line — Atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) + Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) = IMbrave150 (mOS 19.2 vs 13.4 months vs sorafenib); OR durvalumab + tremelimumab (TOPAZ, HIMALAYA). Second-line (post-sorafenib): Regorafenib, Cabozantinib, Ramucirumab (only if AFP ≥400 ng/mL), nivolumab/pembrolizumab. Surveillance: HBsAg carriers ± cirrhosis → 6-monthly USS ± AFP. Milan criteria for transplant: single ≤5 cm OR ≤3 nodules each ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion, no extrahepatic disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Lupus Nephritis — WHO/ISN Classification and Immunopathology
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with SLE (anti-dsDNA positive, anti-Sm positive, low C3/C4) presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria (5.8 g/day), haematuria, red cell casts, and creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL. Renal biopsy on LM shows diffuse proliferative changes affecting >50% of glomeruli, with endocapillary hypercellularity and 'wire-loop' lesions. IF shows full-house pattern (IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, C1q, kappa, lambda). EM shows subendothelial, mesangial, and rare subepithelial deposits. Which of the following statements about this biopsy finding, its immunopathogenesis, and treatment is MOST accurate?

options.A: This is ISN/RPS Class II lupus nephritis (mesangial proliferative); wire-loop lesions indicate mesangial deposits only; treated with hydroxychloroquine alone
options.B: This is ISN/RPS Class IV Lupus Nephritis (Diffuse proliferative LN) — most severe and most common class requiring aggressive treatment; 'wire-loop' lesions = massive subendothelial immune complex deposits lifting the capillary wall (thickened rigid loop on LM); full-house IF (IgG+IgM+IgA+C3+C1q) is characteristic of lupus nephritis; immunopathogenesis: anti-dsDNA + nucleosomal antigens (HMGB1) → immune complexes deposit in glomeruli → classical complement activation (C1q, C4, C3) → MAC formation + neutrophil recruitment → glomerular injury; treatment: induction — mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 2–3 g/day OR cyclophosphamide (NIH/Euro-Lupus protocol) + high-dose steroids; belimumab (anti-BLyS) + MMF as add-on (BLISS-LN); voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor) + MMF + steroids (AURORA trial); maintenance: MMF or azathioprine + low-dose steroids
options.C: This is IgA nephropathy with secondary SLE features; mesangial IgA deposits dominate on IF; treated with ACE inhibitor and fish oil
options.D: This is Class V (membranous) lupus nephritis; subepithelial deposits dominate; 'spike and dome' on silver stain; treated with calcineurin inhibitors alone; no steroid required

questions.explanation: Lupus Nephritis ISN/RPS 2003 Classification: Class I — minimal mesangial LN (normal LM, mesangial deposits on IF/EM); Class II — mesangial proliferative LN (mesangial hypercellularity + mesangial deposits); Class III — focal proliferative LN (<50% glomeruli involved); Class IV — DIFFUSE proliferative LN (≥50% glomeruli; most common class requiring ISN criteria + most severe); Class V — membranous LN (global/segmental subepithelial deposits + GBM thickening; nephrotic syndrome; can coexist with III/IV); Class VI — advanced sclerosing (>90% global glomerulosclerosis). Class IV hallmarks: (1) Wire-loop lesions: massive SUBENDOTHELIAL deposits of immune complexes → thickening + rigidity of capillary walls → eosinophilic hyaline-like 'wire-loops' on H&E; (2) Full-house IF: IgG+IgM+IgA+C3+C4+C1q (classical pathway, C1q fixation diagnostic of lupus over other GN); (3) EM: predominantly subendothelial deposits (+ mesangial, occasional subepithelial); (4) Fibrinoid necrosis, crescents (poor prognosis). Immunopathogenesis: Impaired clearance of apoptotic cells (DNase I deficiency, complement deficiency) → nuclear material (dsDNA, histones, HMGB1, snRNPs) exposed → anti-dsDNA + anti-Sm + other ANA produced → nucleosome-anti-nucleosome complexes deposit in glomerular structures (affinity for GBM heparan sulphate, mesangial matrix) → classical complement → C3a/C5a (anaphylatoxins) + MAC (C5b-9) + FcγR-mediated neutrophil/monocyte activation → glomerular injury. Treatment 2024: Induction — MMF (2–3 g/day) preferred in non-White patients; Low-dose Euro-Lupus cyclophosphamide in White patients; both with high-dose steroids (1 mg/kg/day). Triple therapy: voclosporin (23.7 mg BD) + MMF + low-dose steroids (AURORA-1: superior remission vs MMF + steroids). Belimumab + standard of care (BLISS-LN: superior renal response at 2 years). Maintenance: MMF (preferred) or azathioprine + low-dose prednisolone for minimum 3 years.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Colorectal Carcinoma — Molecular Pathways and Lynch Syndrome
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman is diagnosed with right-sided colon cancer. Her mother had endometrial cancer at 44 years, her brother had colon cancer at 40 years. Her tumour shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression on IHC and microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) status. Which of the following MOST accurately explains the molecular pathogenesis of this cancer syndrome, distinguishes it from sporadic MSI-H CRC, and identifies the optimal systemic treatment for metastatic disease?

options.A: This is familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP); APC mutation; hundreds of polyps; prevented by colectomy; treated with FOLFOX chemotherapy; MSI is absent in FAP
options.B: This is Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): autosomal dominant germline mutation in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes — MLH1 (most common), MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 → defective MMR → accumulation of replication errors at microsatellite sequences (short tandem repeats) → microsatellite instability (MSI-H); Lynch vs sporadic MSI-H: Lynch = germline MMR mutation (constitutional) detected on germline testing; sporadic MSI-H = somatic MLH1 PROMOTER HYPERMETHYLATION (epigenetic silencing, NOT germline) + BRAF V600E mutation (present in ~50% sporadic MSI-H CRC, ABSENT in Lynch); Amsterdam II criteria; Lynch-associated cancers: colon (right-sided, mucinous, poor differentiation, tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes), endometrium, ovary, stomach, ureter, biliary. Metastatic CRC treatment: MMR-deficient/MSI-H — pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) or nivolumab ± ipilimumab (KEYNOTE-177: superior PFS/OS vs chemotherapy as first-line); MMR-proficient/MSS — FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab/cetuximab (RAS/BRAF WT)
options.C: This is MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP); autosomal recessive; biallelic MUTYH germline mutations; MSI-H status absent; treated identically to FAP
options.D: Sporadic CRC and Lynch syndrome CRC are molecularly identical; BRAF V600E mutation is present in all MSI-H CRCs including Lynch syndrome; immunotherapy is not superior to chemotherapy in MSI-H CRC

questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome (Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer — HNPCC): Most common hereditary CRC syndrome (~3–5% of all CRC). Autosomal dominant. MMR genes: MLH1 (most common, ~40%), MSH2 (~30%), MSH6 (~15%), PMS2 (~10%), EPCAM (3' deletion causing MSH2 silencing). Mechanism: Germline MMR mutation → one defective allele inherited; somatic loss of second allele (LOH, methylation) → complete MMR loss → replication errors at microsatellites accumulate (hundreds of replication errors uncorrected per cell cycle) → frameshift mutations in tumour suppressor genes with microsatellite-containing coding regions (e.g., TGFBR2 poly-A tract, BAX, MLH3, MSH3) → tumourigenesis via mutator pathway (NOT APC/β-catenin pathway). Critical distinction — Lynch vs sporadic MSI-H: Lynch: germline mutation confirmed on blood DNA testing (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 sequencing); BRAF V600E ABSENT; methylation of MLH1 promoter ABSENT. Sporadic MSI-H: somatic MLH1 promoter HYPERMETHYLATION (epigenetic, not germline) + BRAF V600E mutation in ~50%; no family history pattern. This is why BRAF V600E testing + MLH1 promoter methylation should be done on all MMR-deficient tumours to distinguish Lynch (germline testing needed) from sporadic. Amsterdam II criteria (clinical diagnosis): ≥3 relatives with Lynch-associated cancer (CRC, endometrial, small bowel, ureter, renal pelvis) in ≥2 successive generations, ≥1 case <50 years, FAP excluded. Bethesda guidelines: trigger MSI testing (less stringent). Treatment: Metastatic MSI-H/dMMR CRC: KEYNOTE-177 — pembrolizumab vs FOLFOX/FOLFIRI: PFS 16.5 vs 8.2 months, ORR 43.8% vs 33.1%; first-line pembrolizumab now standard. Locally advanced Lynch CRC: surveillance colonoscopy every 1–2 years from age 20–25; prophylactic aspirin (Lynch Lynch programme, CAPP2: aspirin 600 mg/day significantly reduces Lynch cancer incidence).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.subtopic: Amyloidosis — Classification, Pathology and Organ Involvement
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old man with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive nephrotic syndrome, hepatosplenomegaly, macroglossia, and diastolic heart failure. Renal biopsy with Congo red staining shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Serum amyloid A (SAA) is markedly elevated. Mass spectrometry of the biopsy confirms AA fibrils. Which of the following MOST accurately explains the molecular basis of amyloid fibril formation, correctly classifies this patient's amyloidosis, differentiates it from AL amyloidosis, and identifies the novel targeted therapy?

options.A: This is AL amyloidosis from plasma cell dyscrasia; light chain lambda predominates; treated with daratumumab-based regimen; serum free light chains are elevated
options.B: This is AA (secondary/reactive) amyloidosis: chronic inflammatory disease (RA, TB, bronchiectasis, osteomyelitis, FMF, IBD) → sustained elevation of serum amyloid A protein (SAA — acute phase reactant synthesised by liver, induced by IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α → SAA cleaved to AA fragment (76 amino acids) by unknown protease → AA undergoes conformational change to beta-pleated sheet fibrils → extracellular deposition in kidney (mesangium, then GBM), spleen (periarteriolar — 'sago spleen'), liver (sinusoids), adrenal glands; Congo red: salmon-pink on LM, apple-green birefringence under cross-polarised light; molecular basis of all amyloids: misfolded proteins adopt cross-β sheet quaternary structure → hydrogen bonds between beta-sheets → protofilaments → fibrils (7–10 nm diameter, unbranched); TREATMENT: (1) Control underlying inflammation (RA — anti-TNF, IL-6 inhibitors → reduce SAA); (2) Eplontersen/inotersen (antisense oligonucleotide) or patisiran (siRNA) for ATTR amyloidosis; (3) Diflunisal — kinetic stabiliser for TTR; (4) Daratumumab-VCd for AL amyloidosis
options.C: This is ATTR (transthyretin) amyloidosis; wild-type TTR deposits in heart (restrictive cardiomyopathy); NOT associated with inflammatory conditions; treated with tafamidis
options.D: All forms of amyloidosis have identical fibril precursor proteins; Congo red is not specific for amyloid; mass spectrometry cannot distinguish AL from AA amyloidosis

questions.explanation: Amyloidosis — comprehensive classification and pathology: Amyloid = extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins in cross-β pleated sheet configuration → form unbranched, non-branching fibrils, 7.5–10 nm diameter. Congo red: salmon-pink on standard LM → apple-green birefringence on cross-polarised light (dichroism from ordered beta-sheet structure). EM: fine fibrils in random array. X-ray: cross-β diffraction pattern. ALL amyloids contain: P-component (serum amyloid P — doughnut-shaped pentamer, stabilises fibrils, target of CPHPC + anti-SAP therapy), apolipoprotein E (APOE). Major types: AL (Primary): precursor — monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (lambda > kappa 2:1); associated with multiple myeloma, MGUS, Waldenström's; organs — heart (restrictive CMP, most common cause of death), kidney (nephrotic), tongue (macroglossia), nerves (peripheral neuropathy), liver. Treatment: daratumumab-VCd (ANDROMEDA trial: superior haematological CR), autologous SCT in eligible patients. AA (Secondary/Reactive): precursor — SAA (serum amyloid A) → cleaved to 76-aa AA fragment; causes — chronic inflammation (RA most common in developed world, TB/leprosy most common in developing world, FMF — MEFV gene mutation), chronic infections (osteomyelitis, bronchiectasis), IBD. Organs: kidney (glomerular deposits → nephrotic syndrome — most common cause of renal involvement in AA), spleen (two patterns: 'sago spleen' = periarteriolar follicular deposits → white irregular foci; 'lardaceous spleen' = red pulp/sinusoidal deposits → entire spleen enlarged and homogeneous), liver, adrenals. Macroglossia: AL > AA. Treatment: control underlying disease (anti-IL-6 for RA → ↓SAA); colchicine (FMF) prevents AA. ATTR amyloidosis: precursor — transthyretin (TTR, transport protein for T4 and retinol); Wild-type ATTR (senile cardiac amyloidosis): elderly men, restrictive CMP, wrist carpal tunnel syndrome, NO inflammatory cause; Hereditary ATTR: Val122Ile mutation (African-American cardiac), Val30Met mutation (peripheral neuropathy). Treatment: Tafamidis (kinetic stabiliser of TTR tetramer — prevents dissociation and misfolding; ATTR-ACT trial: reduced CV mortality in wtATTR/hATTR CMP); Patisiran (siRNA silences TTR in hepatocytes; APOLLO trial: reduced TTR production → ↓neuropathy progression); Eplontersen (antisense oligonucleotide, SubQ monthly, NEURO-TTRansform trial). Gold standard typing: mass spectrometry-based proteomics on biopsy — gold standard to identify precursor protein (distinguishes AL, AA, ATTR, ALect2 amyloidosis). Scintigraphy: 99mTc-DPD/PYP/HMDP scan — ATTR cardiac amyloidosis (high sensitivity/specificity, non-invasive).
